blocks.text: A limit describes the value a function is heading toward as its input gets closer and closer to some target point, whether or not the function ever actually reaches that value at that exact point. It is the very first idea in calculus, and everything else in this module, derivatives, partial derivatives, the chain rule, the gradient, is built directly on top of it.

blocks.alt: x approaching a target point a from the left and from the right, both sides settling on the same limit value L
blocks.caption: A limit asks what value a function is trending toward, not necessarily what value it actually has.

blocks.text: This lesson stays entirely at the conceptual and computational level needed for the rest of this module. The goal is not mastery of every limit law taught in a full calculus course, it is building the specific intuition that makes the formal definition of a derivative, covered in the next lesson, feel inevitable rather than mysterious.
1. The Intuitive Idea of a Limit

Imagine watching the output of a function as its input creeps closer and closer to some specific number, say 2, without ever landing exactly on 2. If the outputs keep settling closer and closer to some single value, say 4, then 4 is called the limit of the function as the input approaches 2.

The key word is approaches. A limit is fundamentally a statement about trend and destination, not about a single computed value at a single point. This distinction feels subtle at first, but it turns out to matter enormously, since some of the most important functions in calculus are undefined exactly at the point you care about.
1.1 A Simple Example Without Formal Language

Consider the function that doubles its input, f of x equals 2 times x. As x creeps toward 3, from 2.9, to 2.99, to 2.999, the output creeps toward 6, from 5.8, to 5.98, to 5.998. There is nothing surprising here, the limit as x approaches 3 is simply 6, matching what you would get by plugging 3 in directly.

This well-behaved case, where the limit simply equals the function value at that point, is the easy case, and it covers a huge fraction of everyday functions. The genuinely interesting cases, covered later in this lesson, are the ones where direct substitution does not work at all.
2. Notation for Limits

The standard way to write a limit uses the abbreviation lim underneath which the input variable and the point it approaches are written, followed by the function itself. Written out in words, it reads limit as x approaches a of f of x, and the whole expression stands for the single value the function trends toward.

code.content:
# In symbolic notation:
#   lim_{x -> a} f(x) = L
# reads: "the limit of f(x), as x approaches a, is L"

import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
f = 2 * x
L = sp.limit(f, x, 3)
print(L)   # 6

blocks.text: 2.1 Reading the Notation Aloud

It helps to practice reading limit notation aloud until it feels ordinary. The arrow inside the notation is read as approaches, never as equals, since x never actually has to equal a for the limit to be perfectly well defined. Only the destination value L is an equals sign away from the whole expression.

items: The subscript under lim names the variable that is moving, almost always x.
The arrow target is the specific point that variable is creeping toward, called a.
The value after the equals sign, L, is what the outputs are trending toward, not necessarily f of a itself.

blocks.text: 3. One-Sided Limits

Sometimes it matters which direction the input is approaching from. A one-sided limit only considers inputs coming from one side of the target point, either strictly below it or strictly above it, and the two directions do not have to agree with each other.
3.1 The Left-Hand Limit

The left-hand limit only looks at inputs smaller than a, creeping upward toward it from below. It is written with a small minus sign attached to a, and it captures what the function is trending toward if you only ever approach from the left side of the number line.

code.content:
# Left-hand limit notation:
#   lim_{x -> a^-} f(x)
# only considers x values less than a, creeping up toward it

blocks.text: 3.2 The Right-Hand Limit
The right-hand limit is the mirror image, only looking at inputs larger than a, creeping downward toward it from above. It is written with a small plus sign attached to a.

code.content:
# Right-hand limit notation:
#   lim_{x -> a^+} f(x)
# only considers x values greater than a, creeping down toward it

blocks.text: One-sided limits matter most for functions that jump or behave differently on either side of a point, step functions, piecewise definitions, and functions with vertical asymptotes are the classic examples where the left and right stories genuinely differ.
4. Limits Do Not Require the Function to Be Defined at the Point

One of the most important, and most counterintuitive, facts about limits is that a function does not need to be defined at a point at all for its limit to exist there. The limit only cares about what happens as you get arbitrarily close to a, never about what happens exactly at a.

Consider f of x equals x squared minus 4, divided by x minus 2. Plugging in x equals 2 directly gives 0 divided by 0, which is undefined, yet the limit as x approaches 2 is a perfectly well defined number, 4, because the function simplifies to x plus 2 everywhere except exactly at x equals 2.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
f = (x**2 - 4) / (x - 2)
print(sp.limit(f, x, 2))   # 4, even though f(2) itself is 0/0, undefined

blocks.title: The gap in the graph is invisible to the limit
blocks.content: A function like this one has a single missing point, a tiny hole, in its graph at x equals 2. The limit completely ignores that hole and reports what the surrounding, well defined values are trending toward.

blocks.text: 5. When a Limit Exists: Both Sides Must Agree

A two-sided limit, the ordinary kind covered throughout most of this lesson, only exists when the left-hand limit and the right-hand limit both exist and are equal to each other. If the two sides trend toward different values, the overall limit at that point simply does not exist.
5.1 A Function Where the Two Sides Disagree

Consider a function that outputs negative 1 for every negative input and positive 1 for every non-negative input, a step right at zero. Approaching zero from the left, the output is stuck at negative 1. Approaching from the right, the output is stuck at positive 1. Since these do not match, the two-sided limit at zero does not exist, even though both one-sided limits individually do.

blocks.text: 6. Computing Limits by Direct Substitution

For the large family of functions that are continuous everywhere, polynomials, most everyday combinations of them, computing a limit is as simple as plugging the target point directly into the function. This works precisely because a continuous function never has any sudden jumps, holes, or breaks for the limit to disagree with.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
f = x**3 - 2*x + 1
print(sp.limit(f, x, 2))     # via the limit machinery
print(f.subs(x, 2))          # direct substitution, same answer: 5

blocks.text: 6.1 Where Direct Substitution Fails

Direct substitution breaks down whenever plugging in the target point produces an undefined expression, most commonly zero divided by zero. That failure is not a sign the limit does not exist, it is a signal that some algebraic rewriting is needed first, exactly the case covered next.
7. Computing Limits That Need Algebraic Simplification

When direct substitution produces a zero over zero form, the standard move is to rewrite the function algebraically, usually by factoring, so that the problematic term cancels out before substituting again. The limit itself never changes value during this process, only the visible form of the expression does.
7.1 Factoring to Cancel a Zero Over Zero Form

Take the earlier example again, x squared minus 4 over x minus 2. Factoring the numerator gives x minus 2 times x plus 2, and the shared x minus 2 factor cancels against the denominator everywhere except exactly at x equals 2, leaving the simple expression x plus 2, into which 2 can now be substituted directly to get 4.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
expr = (x**2 - 4) / (x - 2)
simplified = sp.simplify(expr)
print(simplified)              # x + 2
print(simplified.subs(x, 2))   # 4

blocks.text: This cancel-then-substitute pattern is the workhorse technique for computing limits by hand, and it reappears constantly, in a slightly more elaborate form, in the formal limit definition of the derivative covered in the very next lesson.
8. Limits and Continuity

A function is called continuous at a point precisely when three things all line up, the limit exists there, the function is actually defined there, and the limit equals that defined value. Any break in that chain, a missing point, a jump, or a mismatch, makes the function discontinuous at that point.

items: The limit as x approaches a must exist.
The function value f of a must exist.
The limit and the function value must be equal to each other.

blocks.text: This is precisely why the earlier hole example, x squared minus 4 over x minus 2, is discontinuous at x equals 2, the limit exists and equals 4, but the function itself is simply not defined there at all, so the second condition fails.
9. Limits at Infinity

Limits are not only about approaching a specific finite point, they can also describe what a function trends toward as its input grows without bound, either toward positive infinity or negative infinity. This flavor of limit describes long-run, large-scale behavior rather than local behavior near one point.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
f = 1 / x
print(sp.limit(f, x, sp.oo))    # 0, the function flattens toward zero for huge x

blocks.text: 9.1 Horizontal Asymptotes

When a limit at infinity settles on a finite value, that value describes a horizontal asymptote, a flat line the function hugs more and more closely as its input grows huge in either direction. This idea will resurface later in this platform whenever a saturating function, like a sigmoid activation, is discussed.
10. Piecewise Functions and Limits

Piecewise functions, defined by one formula on one interval and a different formula on another, are the most natural place to see one-sided limits genuinely earn their keep. Checking whether such a function is continuous at the seam between its pieces means checking the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and the function value all at once.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
f = sp.Piecewise((x + 1, x < 1), (3 - x, x >= 1))
left = sp.limit(f, x, 1, dir="-")
right = sp.limit(f, x, 1, dir="+")
print(left, right)   # 2, 2 -- both sides agree, the seam is continuous here

blocks.text: 11. Why Limits Matter: The Foundation of the Derivative

Limits are not taught for their own sake in this module, they exist to make the derivative, covered in the very next lesson, precise. The derivative of a function at a point is defined as the limit of a specific ratio, the change in output divided by the change in input, as that change in input shrinks toward zero without ever actually reaching it.
11.1 Preview: The Difference Quotient

That ratio, f of x plus h minus f of x, all divided by h, is called the difference quotient, and it measures the average slope of the function over a small interval of width h. As h shrinks toward zero, this ratio settles on the instantaneous slope at a single point, but only a limit can make sense of a ratio whose denominator is heading toward zero without ever letting it actually reach zero and produce an undefined division.

blocks.title: Forward reference
blocks.content: The full formal definition of the derivative, built directly from this exact limit, is covered in the next lesson in this module, Derivatives. Everything covered here about one-sided limits, direct substitution, and algebraic simplification gets reused immediately there.

blocks.text: 12. Why AI Practitioners Should Care About Limits

Very little day-to-day machine learning work involves computing limits by hand. The reason this lesson still matters is that limits are the conceptual bedrock underneath the derivative, and the derivative is the conceptual bedrock underneath gradient-based learning, the mechanism training almost every modern neural network.

Understanding limits well enough to see why the derivative is defined the way it is pays off the moment something breaks, a loss that produces not a number, a gradient that explodes near a boundary, an activation function that saturates. Those situations are all, underneath the surface, limit behavior near a specific point or near infinity.
13. A Worked Example
Compute the limit as x approaches 1 of the function x squared plus 3x minus 4, all divided by x minus 1.

Direct substitution first, plugging x equals 1 into the top gives 1 plus 3 minus 4, which is 0, and the bottom gives 1 minus 1, which is also 0. A zero over zero form, so factoring is needed before substituting again.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
numerator = x**2 + 3*x - 4
factored = sp.factor(numerator)
print(factored)   # (x - 1)*(x + 4)

expr = (x**2 + 3*x - 4) / (x - 1)
print(sp.limit(expr, x, 1))   # 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Expression","Result"],"rows":[["Direct substitution","(1 + 3 - 4) / (1 - 1)","0 / 0, undefined"],["Factor numerator","(x - 1)(x + 4) / (x - 1)","cancels to x + 4"],["Substitute again","1 + 4","5"]]}

blocks.text: So the limit is exactly 5, even though the original expression is undefined precisely at x equals 1, the same hole-in-the-graph situation covered earlier in this lesson.
14. Practice
Before checking the answer, try computing the limit as x approaches 3 of x squared minus 9, all divided by x minus 3, by hand using the factor-and-cancel technique from this lesson.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
expr = (x**2 - 9) / (x - 3)
print(sp.limit(expr, x, 3))

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: x squared minus 9 factors into x minus 3 times x plus 3. Cancelling the shared x minus 3 factor leaves x plus 3, and substituting 3 gives 6. The limit is 6.

blocks.text: 14.1 A Second Exercise: One-Sided Limits

Using the absolute value function, f of x equals the absolute value of x, divided by x, compute the left-hand limit and the right-hand limit separately as x approaches 0, and decide whether the two-sided limit exists.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: For x greater than 0, the absolute value of x equals x, so the ratio is 1. For x less than 0, the absolute value of x equals negative x, so the ratio is negative 1. The left-hand limit is negative 1, the right-hand limit is 1, they disagree, so the two-sided limit at 0 does not exist.

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a limit requires the function to be defined at that exact point, it does not.
Stopping after direct substitution produces zero over zero and wrongly concluding the limit does not exist, instead of simplifying algebraically first.
Confusing the value a function actually outputs at a point with the value its limit trends toward there, they can differ.
Forgetting to check whether the left-hand and right-hand limits agree before claiming a two-sided limit exists.
Treating limits at infinity as a fundamentally different topic, rather than the same core idea of trending toward a value, just as the input grows huge instead of approaching a finite point.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes trace back to treating a limit as if it were simple substitution. It usually is, for well behaved continuous functions, but the entire reason limits deserve their own lesson is the handful of cases where substitution alone is not enough.
Key Takeaway

A limit describes the value a function trends toward as its input approaches some point, whether from the left, from the right, or from both directions at once, and critically, without ever requiring the function to actually be defined at that exact point. Direct substitution handles the easy, continuous cases, while factoring and simplification handle the zero-over-zero cases that show up constantly in more interesting problems.

This idea exists in this module for one overriding reason, it makes the derivative, covered next, precise. The derivative is defined as the limit of a ratio as a small change in input shrinks toward zero, and every technique covered in this lesson, one-sided limits, algebraic simplification, checking whether both sides agree, gets reused immediately in that definition.
